content: The law of conservation of mass, also referred to as the law of mass or matter conservation, states that the mass of a closed system remains constant, regardless of the processes occurring within the system. This principle implies that matter cannot be created or destroyed, although it can be rearranged. In any chemical process within a closed system, the total mass of the reactants must equal the total mass of the products. The concept of matter conservation, in the sense of particle conservation, is an approximate physical law that holds true only in the classical sense, prior to the development of special relativity and quantum mechanics. In open systems, where energy can enter or leave the system, mass is not generally conserved. However, in modern physics, the law of mass conservation for closed systems, when viewed from their center of momentum inertial frames, remains valid. This principle has been historically significant and is widely applied in fields such as chemistry, mechanics, and fluid dynamics. An early but incomplete theory of mass conservation was proposed by Nasīr al-Dīn al-Tūsī in the 13th century. He stated that a body of matter can change but cannot disappear. The law of conservation of mass was first clearly formulated by Antoine Lavoisier in 1789, earning him the title of the father of modern chemistry. However, Mikhail Lomonosov had previously expressed similar ideas in 1748 and demonstrated them experimentally. Other scientists, such as Joseph Black, Henry Cavendish, and Jean Rey, also anticipated Lavoisier's work. Historically, the understanding of mass and weight conservation was obscured for centuries due to the buoyant effect of Earth's atmosphere on the weight of gases. This effect was not fully understood until the invention of the vacuum pump, which allowed for the accurate weighing of gases. Once this was understood, the conservation of mass became a cornerstone in the transition from alchemy to modern chemistry. Scientists realized that substances never disappeared from measurement when buoyancy was accounted for, enabling them to conduct quantitative studies of substance transformations. This law is now a fundamental principle used by scientists worldwide. In the context of special relativity, the conservation of mass does not hold. The classical principle that the mass of a system of particles equals the sum of their individual masses is not valid in special relativity. The mass-energy equivalence formula demonstrates that bound systems have a mass less than the sum of their parts. This difference, known as the mass defect, represents the binding energy—the energy required to separate the components of the system. The greater the mass defect, the stronger the binding energy. When the components combine to form a bound system, the binding energy is released, and the system's mass decreases as energy exits the system. The conservation of mass can be reframed in terms of the conservation of a system's combined energy and momentum, which remains conserved and provides the same invariant mass for any system, regardless of the observer. This principle applies to particles created through pair production, as the invariant mass of closed systems does not change when new particles are formed.
